title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: SCOPE AND HOW TO APPLY THIS SUMMARY
text: This document summarizes U.S. DOT guidance. Do not apply these U.S. rules automatically to a flight that is not covered by the U.S. rules. Check whether the itinerary is a covered scheduled flight to, from, or within the United States and whether the airline or ticket agent is the merchant of record for the payment. The merchant of record is generally the entity shown on the passenger's payment statement.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text: For a covered flight cancelled by the airline, a consumer who chooses not to travel or not to accept an offered travel credit, voucher, or other compensation may be entitled to a refund of the ticket price. The reason for the cancellation does not by itself remove the refund right when the consumer chooses not to travel. Apply the detailed DOT and eCFR conditions, including the merchant-of-record rules.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: SIGNIFICANT DELAY OR SCHEDULE CHANGE — LATE ARRIVAL
text:
For a domestic itinerary, the late arrival test is met when, because of a delay or change made by the covered carrier, the consumer is scheduled to arrive at the destination airport 3 hours or more after the original scheduled arrival time. For an international itinerary, the late arrival threshold is 6 hours or more after the original scheduled arrival time.

IMPORTANT: compare the ORIGINAL SCHEDULED ARRIVAL with the REVISED SCHEDULED ARRIVAL communicated by the airline. The rule's late-arrival definition uses when the consumer is scheduled to arrive. A flight that actually lands 3.5 hours late, without information showing that the airline's revised schedule met the scheduled-arrival threshold, does not by itself establish this particular significant-change trigger. Do not silently substitute actual arrival time for revised scheduled arrival time.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: SIGNIFICANT DELAY OR SCHEDULE CHANGE — LATE ARRIVAL
text: A departure that is 3 or 4 hours late is not the same as a late-arrival trigger. A delayed departure may or may not result in a scheduled arrival that is at least 3 hours later. Assess the revised scheduled arrival separately.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text:
The DOT definition also includes certain other carrier-made itinerary changes, including:

- Scheduled early departure at least 3 hours earlier for a domestic itinerary or at least 6 hours earlier for an international itinerary.

- A different origin airport or destination airport.

- More connection points than the original itinerary.

- An involuntary downgrade to a lower class of service.

- Certain changes to connecting airports or aircraft accessibility features for a passenger with a disability.

Check the detailed rule for the precise conditions. Early departure means leaving earlier than originally scheduled; it does not mean a departure that is late.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: NON-REFUNDABLE TICKET — REFUND WHEN THE PASSENGER DOES NOT TRAVEL
text:
14 CFR §260.6(a) specifically addresses a consumer holding a nonrefundable ticket on a covered scheduled flight to, from, or within the United States. A covered carrier that is the merchant of record must provide a full and prompt refund of airfare, including applicable taxes and ancillary fees, when the flight is cancelled or significantly delayed/changed and the consumer chooses not to fly on the affected flight or accept rebooking on an alternative flight, and does not accept a voucher, credit, or other compensation offered as an explicit alternative to the refund.

Do not state that every passenger with a non-refundable ticket automatically receives a refund after any delay. First establish that the flight was cancelled or significantly delayed/changed under the applicable definition and that the consumer did not take the affected or alternative transportation or accept compensation in place of the refund.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: IF THE PASSENGER REJECTS AN OFFER OR DOES NOT RESPOND
text:
Under the automatic-refund provisions, a refund is due in the circumstances described by the rule, including when the consumer rejects the significantly delayed/changed flight, alternative flight, or offered compensation. If the consumer does not respond to an offer of the changed/alternative flight and that flight departs without the consumer, or does not respond to a voucher/credit/compensation offer by the relevant scheduled departure date, the automatic-refund provisions may apply. Silence alone must not be described as an automatic refund without checking the precise offer and departure conditions.

If a passenger intends to travel on the changed or rebooked flight, the passenger should tell the airline before the response deadline stated in the offer. Do not infer acceptance or rejection from incomplete facts.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: INVOLUNTARY DOWNGRADE — CONTINUED TRAVEL AND FARE DIFFERENCE
text:
The U.S. DOT Refunds page identifies an involuntary move to a lower class of service as a significant change. If the passenger chooses not to travel or not to accept travel credits, vouchers, or other compensation offered by the airline because of the involuntary downgrade, the DOT page states that a refund may be due under the applicable conditions.

If the downgraded passenger continues to travel on the flight, the U.S. DOT states that the passenger is not entitled to a refund of the full airfare, but the airline must refund the difference between the original fare and the downgraded fare. This is a fare-difference remedy, not a full ticket refund.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: INVOLUNTARY DOWNGRADE — CONTINUED TRAVEL AND FARE DIFFERENCE
text: The U.S. DOT Refunds page's downgrade explanation does not state a separate processing deadline for this fare-difference refund. Do not automatically apply the 7-business-day or 20-calendar-day prompt-refund deadlines for a ticket-price refund to the fare difference unless a retrieved source expressly establishes that the deadline applies to this remedy. Do not invent a fare difference amount or a processing deadline.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: IF THE PASSENGER ACCEPTS OR USES THE CHANGED FLIGHT
text:
A consumer who chooses to take the significantly delayed/changed flight or an alternative flight offered by the airline generally is not entitled to a refund of the full ticket price under the DOT significant-delay/change refund rule. Do not tell a passenger who completed the changed or alternative trip that they automatically qualify for a full ticket refund merely because the actual arrival was late.

A completed journey does not rule out every other possible remedy. For example, when a passenger is involuntarily downgraded and continues to travel, DOT guidance says the passenger is generally entitled to the difference between the original fare and the downgraded fare, rather than a refund of the full airfare. Other airline commitments or applicable rules may also be relevant; retrieve a supporting source before stating them.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text: DOT separately states that a consumer who purchases a fully refundable ticket is entitled to a refund when the consumer does not use the purchased ticket. Keep this separate from the specific non-refundable-ticket obligation in 14 CFR §260.6(a). Do not imply that §260.6(a) is written as a rule covering both fare types in the same way. Check the ticket's terms and whether the ticket was used.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text: 14 CFR §260.6(b) contains separate refund provisions for certain significant changes affecting a passenger with a disability and accessibility features needed by that passenger. If the user raises such circumstances, retrieve and explain the relevant provision; do not assume the general non-refundable-ticket rule is the only provision that may apply.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text: A required refund is generally returned to the original form of payment. The regulatory definition of a prompt refund is within 7 business days after the applicable earliest date for a credit-card purchase, and within 20 calendar days for cash, check, debit card, or other payment methods. Never label the 20-day period as a business-day period. Explain the applicable trigger date carefully: for example, DOT guidance distinguishes the date the passenger rejects an offer from the later departure date when the passenger does not respond and does not use the alternative flight.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: VOUCHERS, CREDITS, AND OTHER COMPENSATION OFFERED IN PLACE OF A REFUND
text: A covered carrier may offer a voucher, credit, or other compensation as an explicit alternative to a refund only under the conditions in the regulation. The offer must clearly and conspicuously disclose the consumer's right to a full refund. Such an alternative must remain valid and redeemable for at least five years, and the consumer must be notified of its expiration date. Do not say that the mere mention of a voucher automatically cancels the passenger's refund right. Determine whether the passenger affirmatively accepted the alternative and check the applicable conditions.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: TICKETS PURCHASED THROUGH AN AGENT OR ONLINE TRAVEL AGENCY
text: The merchant of record is the entity shown on the passenger's financial statement for the ticket payment. If an online travel agency or other ticket agent is the merchant of record, that entity may be responsible for issuing the proper refund. Do not automatically direct every passenger to the airline without checking who processed the payment; explain that the passenger may need to contact the merchant of record and the airline.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: WHAT THIS RULE DOES NOT ESTABLISH
text: A refund right is not the same as a right to extra cash compensation. Do not invent a universal cash-compensation amount for a delay. Meals, hotels, ground transportation, rebooking, and other services may depend on separate airline commitments, the cause of the disruption, and other applicable rules. Retrieve the airline's official commitment source before describing a particular airline's promise.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: FACTS NEEDED FOR A CASE-SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT
text: When these details are missing and they materially affect the answer, establish: (1) whether the itinerary is covered by U.S. DOT rules; (2) whether the airline cancelled or changed the schedule; (3) the original and revised scheduled arrival times, or the other relevant significant change; (4) whether the passenger flew on the changed flight or an alternative flight, rejected it, or did not respond and did not travel; (5) whether the ticket was non-refundable or fully refundable; and (6) who was the merchant of record. Do not ask for information that is not needed to answer the user's question.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
text: For the definition of a significantly delayed or changed flight, see 14 CFR §260.2. For the covered carrier's refund obligation for a non-refundable ticket and related automatic-refund provisions, see 14 CFR §260.6. The DOT refund page is public-facing guidance. These local documents are educational summaries, not verbatim copies of DOT material or legal advice. Consult the linked official source and current eCFR text for the complete rules, conditions, and exceptions. Do not cite 14 CFR §250.13 as the refund authority.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: FULLY REFUNDABLE TICKET — PROCESSING DEADLINE LIMITS
text:
The U.S. DOT Refunds page states that consumers who purchase fully refundable tickets are entitled to a refund when they do not use the purchased ticket. Keep this rule separate from 14 CFR §260.6(a)(1), which specifically addresses a consumer holding a nonrefundable ticket on a covered scheduled flight that is cancelled or significantly delayed/changed and who chooses not to travel or accept an alternative or compensation in lieu of the refund.

The cited DOT page does not state a separate processing deadline in its fully-refundable-ticket explanation for a passenger who voluntarily does not use the ticket. Do not automatically apply the 7-business-day or 20-calendar-day prompt-refund periods in 14 CFR Part 260 to this scenario unless another retrieved source expressly establishes that they apply. Do not invent a deadline.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: FULLY REFUNDABLE TICKET — PROCESSING DEADLINE LIMITS
text: This section concerns the ticket price. Do not assume that every optional ancillary service fee (for example, baggage, seat selection, or lounge access) is automatically refundable under the fully-refundable-ticket statement. Check the separate DOT guidance for the particular ancillary service.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: AUTOMATIC REFUND — NO RESPONSE TO AN ALTERNATIVE-FLIGHT OFFER
text:
Under 14 CFR §260.6(a)(2)(iii)(A), when a consumer does not respond to an offer of a significantly delayed or changed flight or an alternative flight, the automatic-refund condition includes that the offered flight departs without the consumer. Do not state that silence alone is sufficient before checking that departure condition and that the underlying flight qualifies for a refund under the applicable rule.

The U.S. DOT Refunds page explains that when the consumer does not respond to an alternative-transportation offer and does not fly on the offered alternative, the refund is due to the original form of payment within 7 business days for credit-card payments or 20 calendar days for other payment methods after the significantly delayed or changed flight or the alternative flight departs from its destination. For an explicit rejection, the DOT page describes the deadline as running from the date the consumer rejects the offer.

title: U.S. DOT — Refunds (local educational summary)
section: AUTOMATIC REFUND — NO RESPONSE TO AN ALTERNATIVE-FLIGHT OFFER
text:
A different no-response condition applies to an offer of voucher, credit, or other compensation. Under 14 CFR §260.6(a)(2)(iii)(B), check whether the consumer failed to respond by the date on which the cancelled flight was scheduled to depart or the date the significantly delayed or changed flight departs. Do not reuse the alternative-flight departure trigger for this voucher/credit scenario.

OFFICIAL SOURCES: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-260/section-260.6 and https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/aviation-consumer-protection/refunds

title: U.S. DOT — Tarmac Delays (local educational summary)
text: A tarmac delay occurs when an aircraft is on the ground, either waiting to take off or after landing, and passengers do not have an opportunity to get off the plane. The DOT tarmac-delay rule applies to covered carriers at U.S. airports. Waiting in the terminal or at a gate is not, by itself, a tarmac delay.

title: U.S. DOT — Tarmac Delays (local educational summary)
text:
For flights departing from a U.S. airport, airlines must begin moving the aircraft to a place where passengers can safely get off before 3 hours for domestic flights and before 4 hours for international flights. For arriving flights landing at U.S. airports, passengers must be given an opportunity to safely get off before 3 hours for domestic flights and before 4 hours for international flights.

Exceptions to the time limits are allowed for safety, security, or air-traffic-control reasons. Passengers should not leave the aircraft unless the airline tells them it is safe. The airline is not required to let a passenger back on the aircraft after the passenger chooses to get off during a tarmac delay.

title: U.S. DOT — Tarmac Delays (local educational summary)
text: During a covered tarmac delay, airlines must provide a snack and drinking water no later than 2 hours after the start of the tarmac delay. The rule does not require a full meal during a tarmac delay. Food and water may be withheld only when the pilot determines service cannot be provided for safety or security reasons.

title: U.S. DOT — Tarmac Delays (local educational summary)
text: During a tarmac delay, airlines must provide working toilets, comfortable cabin temperatures, and adequate medical attention when needed. Airlines must notify passengers about the status of the delay when the tarmac delay exceeds 30 minutes. If passengers can safely leave, the airline must timely notify them of the opportunity.

title: U.S. DOT — Tarmac Delays (local educational summary)
text: The 3-hour domestic and 4-hour international limits concern the opportunity to leave an aircraft during a covered tarmac delay. They do not mean that every 3- or 4-hour delay while waiting in an airport terminal automatically creates a federal right to a hotel or meal under the tarmac-delay rule. For terminal delays, check the airline's customer-service commitments and the separate DOT refund rules.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
text: The U.S. DOT dashboard describes services airlines commit to provide when a delay or cancellation is caused by circumstances within the airline's control. Examples given by DOT include maintenance or crew problems, cabin cleaning, baggage loading, and fueling. These commitments should not be described as automatic benefits for every delay, including delays caused by weather or other circumstances outside airline control.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
text:
The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to rebook passengers on the same airline at no additional cost for significant controllable delays.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to rebook passengers on a partner airline, or another airline with which it has an agreement, at no additional cost for significant controllable delays.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to provide a meal or meal cash/voucher when a flight delay results in a passenger waiting 3 hours or more. This is a waiting-time condition for meal assistance. It is not the federal refund threshold and must not be confused with the late-arrival test used by the DOT refund rule.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to complimentary hotel accommodations and ground transportation to and from the hotel for passengers affected by an overnight controllable delay.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
text: The dashboard does not mark American Airlines as committed to cash compensation, a credit or travel voucher, or frequent-flyer miles when a controllable delay results in a passenger waiting 3 hours or more from the scheduled departure time. Do not convert this absence of a dashboard commitment into a claim that a passenger can never receive a discretionary offer or other remedy under a different rule or policy.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
section: IMPORTANT DISTINCTION — REFUND VS. SERVICE COMMITMENT
text: A federal DOT refund right is separate from an airline's service commitments. For a domestic itinerary, the refund significant-delay test is based on scheduled arrival at least 3 hours later than the original scheduled arrival time, and the passenger must choose not to travel or accept the alternative offered. The AA meal commitment instead uses a wait of 3 hours or more. A 4-hour arrival delay does not by itself prove that the passenger waited 3 hours at the airport; assess the actual waiting condition separately.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
section: SIGNIFICANT DELAY IS NOT A UNIVERSAL 3-HOUR RULE
text: The dashboard describes no-cost rebooking for "significant delays" but does not set a universal numeric 3-hour definition for every significant controllable delay. Do not infer such a definition from the separate 3-hour meal-wait commitment or from the federal refund threshold.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
text: The U.S. DOT dashboard states that airlines are required to adhere to the promises in their customer service plans and that DOT will hold airlines accountable if they fail to fulfill a commitment. DOT advises passengers to contact the airline first; if dissatisfied with the airline's response or conduct, the passenger may file a complaint with DOT. Do not claim that enforcement is exclusively internal or that DOT has no role in accountability.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines (local summary)
text: This is an educational local summary, not legal advice. The dashboard is a summary of airline commitments, not a statement that every delay qualifies. Check the live DOT dashboard and American Airlines customer service plan for any later changes before presenting this summary as current policy.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The definition applies to a covered flight itinerary operated or marketed by a covered carrier to, from, or within the United States, subject to the full regulatory definition and any applicable conditions.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: 14 CFR §260.2 defines a significantly delayed or changed flight as a covered itinerary with a delay or change made by a covered carrier where, as a result, one or more listed conditions applies.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
section: LATE ARRIVAL — SCHEDULED ARRIVAL, NOT ACTUAL LANDING TIME
text:
For a domestic itinerary, the consumer must be scheduled to arrive at the destination airport 3 hours or more after the original scheduled arrival time. For an international itinerary, the consumer must be scheduled to arrive 6 hours or more after the original scheduled arrival time.

Compare the original scheduled arrival with the revised scheduled arrival resulting from the carrier's delay or change. The wording is about when the consumer is scheduled to arrive. A plane's actual landing time being 3 hours late, by itself, is not the same as proof that the revised schedule met this definition. Do not replace revised scheduled arrival with actual arrival when applying this specific threshold.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The definition also includes a departure scheduled at least 3 hours earlier than the original scheduled departure for a domestic itinerary, or at least 6 hours earlier for an international itinerary. Early departure means earlier than the original schedule; it does not mean a departure that is late.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text:
- The consumer is scheduled to depart from a different origin airport or arrive at a different destination airport.

- The consumer is scheduled to travel on an itinerary with more connection points than the original itinerary.

- The consumer is involuntarily downgraded to a lower class of service.

- For an individual with a disability, certain changes to connecting airports or substitute aircraft that make needed accessibility features unavailable.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The definition of prompt refund specifies 7 business days after the applicable earliest date for credit-card purchases and 20 calendar days after the applicable earliest date for cash, check, debit card, or other payment methods. See the refund provision and official DOT guidance for the event-specific starting date. Do not call 20 calendar days 20 business days.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The definition in §260.2 is not itself the full refund obligation. For refund eligibility and the covered carrier's obligations for a non-refundable ticket, see 14 CFR §260.6. Also consult the U.S. DOT Refunds page for consumer-facing explanations, fully refundable tickets, downgrades, alternative flights, and refund processing.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: This file is a concise educational summary, not legal advice and not a verbatim reproduction of the regulation. Consult the linked eCFR section for complete text, conditions, exceptions, and current amendments.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text:
The text of 14 CFR §260.6(a)(1) specifically addresses a consumer holding a NONREFUNDABLE ticket on a scheduled flight to, from, or within the United States. A covered carrier that is the merchant of record must provide a full and prompt refund of airfare, including applicable taxes and ancillary fees, for a cancelled or significantly delayed/changed flight when the consumer chooses not to:

- Fly on the significantly delayed or changed flight or accept rebooking on an alternative flight; and

- Accept a voucher, credit, or other form of compensation offered as an explicit alternative to the refund under paragraph (c).

Do not rewrite this subsection as though it expressly applies to refundable and non-refundable fares in an identical way. Fully refundable tickets are addressed separately in U.S. DOT consumer guidance: consumers who purchase a fully refundable ticket are entitled to a refund when they do not use the purchased ticket. Cite the DOT Refunds page for that separate point.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text:
The provision identifies circumstances in which a full refund is due automatically, including:

- A cancelled flight where the consumer is not offered an alternative flight or voucher/credit/other compensation under the relevant provision.

- The consumer rejects the significantly delayed or changed flight, a rebooking on an alternative flight, or a voucher/credit/other offered compensation.

- The consumer does not respond to an offer of the significantly delayed/changed flight or an alternative flight and the offered flight departs without the consumer; or does not respond to an offer of voucher, credit, or other compensation by the date specified in the regulation.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: Do not state that any silence in any situation automatically creates a refund. Establish what offer was made, whether the relevant departure date passed, and whether the passenger used the affected or alternative transportation. DOT's public guidance explains that when a consumer does not respond to an alternative-flight offer and does not fly on the offered alternative, the refund is issued automatically.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: The regulation has separate refund provisions for an individual with a disability who does not want to continue travel because specified significant changes make needed accessibility features unavailable, and for certain other passengers in the same reservation. When the user's circumstances involve disability or accessibility, retrieve and explain the exact subsection rather than applying only the general rule in paragraph (a).

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
section: VOUCHER OR CREDIT AS AN EXPLICIT ALTERNATIVE
text: A covered carrier may offer a voucher, credit, or other compensation as an explicit alternative to a refund required by paragraph (a) only if the offer clearly and conspicuously notifies the consumer of the right to a full refund and the applicable offer terms, and the alternative remains valid and redeemable for at least five years. The carrier must notify the recipient of the expiration date. Do not state that merely receiving or hearing about a voucher automatically waives a refund right; determine whether the consumer accepted the alternative and check the complete rule.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
section: TICKET AGENTS AND MERCHANT OF RECORD
text: When a ticket agent is the merchant of record, the regulation describes the carrier's obligations to notify the agent about refund eligibility and, in specified circumstances, transfer funds to the ticket agent. For a passenger who booked through an online travel agency or another ticket agent, determine who appears as merchant of record on the payment statement before saying which entity processes the refund.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
section: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE PASSENGER TRAVELS
text: A passenger who chooses to take the significantly delayed/changed flight or an alternative flight generally is not entitled to a refund of the full ticket price under the ordinary DOT significant-delay/change rule. Do not equate an actual late arrival with a full refund entitlement after travel has been completed. Certain different remedies may exist; for example, DOT guidance says an involuntary downgrade followed by continued travel generally entitles the passenger to the difference between the original and downgraded fare, not the full airfare. Apply an independently retrieved source to that fact pattern.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: For the definition of a significantly delayed or changed flight, including the scheduled-arrival thresholds of 3 hours domestic and 6 hours international, see 14 CFR §260.2. The same section defines prompt refund as 7 business days after the applicable earliest date for credit-card purchases and 20 calendar days for cash, check, debit card, or other payment methods. The applicable starting date may differ depending on whether the passenger rejects an offer or does not respond and does not use the alternative transportation. Return the refund to the original form of payment as described in DOT guidance.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: This file is a concise educational summary, not legal advice and not a verbatim reproduction of the regulation. The regulation is limited to covered carriers and covered scheduled flights. Consult the linked eCFR section and U.S. DOT Refunds page for complete text, definitions, conditions, exceptions, and current amendments. Do not cite 14 CFR §250.13 as the refund authority.
